statement: England and Burgundy maintained a close alliance during the critical phase of the Hundred Years' War (1419–1435), following the Burgundian-English Treaty of Troyes (1420) that made Henry V heir to France. Philip the Good's alliance with England after the murder of his father John the Fearless (allegedly organized by the Dauphin, future Charles VII) at Montereau (1419) gave England the crucial French partnership that produced the Treaty of Troyes. The alliance held as long as Philip's personal grievance motivated it; the Congress of Arras (1435) reconciled Burgundy and France, decisively undermining the English position and beginning the final phase of French recovery.
